entry.title: JWT and Session Tokens Explained: Stateless vs. Stateful Authentication
entry.summary: Two articles back, we covered cookie+nonce authentication, and last time we looked at how WordPress's login cookie is actually a hybrid: signature verification is fully self-contained, but revocation depends on a server-side list of valid tokens. This time we look at the opposite end of the design spectrum: JWT (JSON Web Token), which aims for authentication that is fully stateless — no server-side token list at all. Comparing it against WordPress's hybrid model makes the trade-off between stateful and stateless authentication much easier to see. A JWT looks like a single string split into three parts by dots — xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz. These correspond to a header, a payload, and a signature. A delivery moves from Tuesday to Thursday. The person who moved it knows. The customer who planned their week around Tuesday does not. Neither does the colleague who promised to be there to receive it. Nothing went wrong in the work itself. The failure was a message that did not get sent.

entry.title: Multi-tenant SaaS with branch-level RBAC in Next.js + Node: a practical architecture
entry.summary: Tenant scoping that fails closed, permissions that know about branches, and the tests that keep both honest. Key takeaways Resolve the tenant from the session, never from the request. A URL slug or header can select which of your memberships to use, but the server must verify that membership. Next.js middleware is a gate, not a guard. Use it for redirects and cheap checks; do real authorization next to the data, in your Node API or server code. Every Server Action and Route Handler is a public endpoint. Authorize inside each one, every time. Make the database refuse cross-tenant reads. PostgreSQL row-level security with a transaction-local setting means a forgotten filter returns nothing instead of someone else's data. Permissions are (action, scope), not role names. entry.title: Express.js Transactional Email Service Wrapper: 5 Retry and Logging Layers
entry.summary: A welcome email should leave the request path quickly, but accepting a job is not the same as delivering a message. The reliable design is a small Node.js service wrapper around a direct email API, backed by a durable queue, a suppression check, stored provider message IDs, and polling for delivery events. Do not build this around SMTP when the chosen capability is API-only. The API boundary gives the application enough structure to decide what may be retried and what must be suppressed. TL;DR: enqueue one idempotent welcome-email job, check suppression immediately before each send, persist the returned message ID, and poll message events into a local delivery record. A bounce should update suppression before another queued job can target that address. This favors correctness over instant …

entry.title: I built a face-rating tool that never sees your photo — here's what I learned about on-device ML

Why I Built This
A friend told me his face shape was better than mine. I'm not going to argue with him — I have no data. So I went looking for one of those "what's your face shape" tools. Every single one wanted me to upload a photo of my face. To a server. Run by someone I don't know. Look, I'm a developer. I know what happens to uploaded images.
